screens.title: Verilog for Sequential Logic: always @(posedge clk) and FSMs
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we learn how synchronous behavior is described in Verilog using the always at positive edge of the clock construct. You will see how every assignment to a reg inside a clocked always block implies one or more flip-flops and how non‑blocking assignment models the simultaneous update of hardware. We will walk through concrete modules: a D flip‑flop, an enabled register, an 8‑bit counter with a synchronous reset, and a traffic light finite state machine written in the common two‑block style. You will also learn the recommended three‑block FSM pattern for clarity and when a Moore or a Mealy style is appropriate. Practical implications are emphasized: why synchronous resets are usually preferred in FPGA flows, why localparam is preferred for state encoding, and how to interpret behavior in simulation versus real silicon. By the end you will be ready to design registers, counters, and robust FSMs and to implement a sequence detector as a hands‑on exercise. Think about where simultaneous updates and clocked behavior are crucial in your design — that is the central idea we will return to throughout the lesson.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you'll be able to express synchronous sequential logic correctly in Verilog and verify it. First, you will write always @(posedge clk) blocks that infer flip‑flops and use non‑blocking assignment so multiple registers update simultaneously. Second, you'll implement registers with clock enables and counters with synchronous resets, understanding how enable and reset signals control captured values in hardware. Third, you'll design finite state machines using the recommended patterns: either the three‑always‑block style for explicit separation of state, next‑state, and outputs, or the common two‑block approach for compact designs. Finally, you'll distinguish Moore and Mealy machines and choose the one that best fits timing and output stability needs. Each objective includes a verification milestone: simulate a D flip‑flop update, test an enabled register with toggled enable, reset and step a counter under a synchronous reset, and simulate the traffic light FSM and a sequence detector to confirm correct outputs. This ensures you not only write code, but also validate timing and behavior in a simulator or on hardware.

screens.title: Objectives: practice and verification
screens.narratorSegment: Let's expand the objectives into testable checks so you know when you have achieved them. For clocked always blocks, success means writing a D flip‑flop module and observing q follow d only on rising clock edges in simulation. For registers and enables, success is toggling the enable signal while stepping the clock and confirming q holds when enable is low and updates when enable is high. For counters and resets, success is asserting the synchronous reset and seeing the counter return to zero only at a clock edge, and verifying the counter increments when enable is high. For FSMs, success is creating a module where state advances according to inputs and the output encoding matches the state table; simulate a traffic light FSM to observe the expected 001, 010, 100 patterns. For Moore vs Mealy, success is demonstrating an output that either changes only on the clock edge or that can change combinationally with inputs. These verification checks ensure design intent matches both simulation and hardware assumptions.

screens.title: always @(posedge clk): the clocked always block
screens.narratorSegment: A clocked always block in Verilog is written as always @(posedge clk) and it tells the simulator and synthesis tools to execute the block at each rising edge of the clock. Practically, every assignment to a reg inside such a block infers a hardware flip‑flop that captures the right‑hand side value at that instant. This is the basic mechanism you use to hold state across cycles. For example, a D flip‑flop module assigns q <= d in an always @(posedge clk) block; when the clock rises, q takes the current value of d. The key reason we use this style is that real flip‑flops on an FPGA capture inputs synchronously on the clock edge; modeling that behavior accurately in code ensures simulation maps to hardware. A common misconception is to think the order of statements inside the block controls update timing—because with non‑blocking assignment all left‑hand sides update simultaneously at the end of the time step. Practically, this means you can compute next‑state expressions using current state and inputs within the same block and rely on simultaneous update semantics to preserve correctness. Consider this teaching check: simulate a D flip‑flop while toggling d asynchronously, and observe q only changes when the clock rises. That observation ties the concept to real behavior and prevents subtle race conditions in complex designs.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: always @(posedge clk) schedules register updates on rising clock edges and models flip‑flop capture.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Clocked always block
What it means
The block executes at each rising clock edge and infers flip‑flops for reg assignments.
Concrete example
// D flip-flop
always @(posedge clk) begin
  q <= d;
end
Simulate toggling d while clock runs and observe q update only when clock rises.
Common misconception
Order of non‑blocking assignments does not create sequential delays; all left‑hand sides update together at the end of the time step.
Pro tip

Use clocked always blocks consistently for all state registers so timing is uniform across the design.

Teaching visual
Simulated waveform scenario
Clock rising edges capture d into q. Toggling d between edges does not affect q until the next edge.
Try: toggle d and step the clock to observe capture.
Why this matches hardware
Flip‑flops in FPGAs latch inputs on the clock edge. Modeling that behavior in Verilog using always @(posedge clk) ensures simulation maps to silicon.
Closing thought: How does simultaneous update simplify next‑state computation?
Key Takeaway
Use always @(posedge clk) to model flip‑flop capture; expect simultaneous updates when using non‑blocking assignments.

screens.title: Non‑blocking assignment (<=) and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: Non‑blocking assignment, the <= operator, is essential inside clocked always blocks because it models how hardware updates multiple flip‑flops at the same instant. When you use <=, the right‑hand sides are evaluated immediately using current signals, but the left‑hand sides are updated later, effectively at the end of the simulation time step. This leads to simultaneous capture semantics: two registers assigned in the same block do not see each other's new values in that cycle. For example, if you compute next_a <= b and next_b <= a in the same clocked block, each right‑hand side reads the old values of a and b, and both update together on the clock. A common pitfall is using blocking assignment, equals, inside a sequential block; that causes sequential updates where the second assignment can observe the first's new value and simulation no longer matches hardware. The practical consequence is subtle functional differences and potential combinational loops or unintended data dependencies in simulation. A quick test to reveal this is to implement two registers where one is assigned from the other and toggle the source for a few cycles; using <= will keep behavior consistent and predictable. To summarize, prefer <= in always @(posedge clk) blocks for all reg updates, unless you are explicitly creating temporary combinational variables for next‑state calculation outside of sequential assignments.

keyIdea.title: Why <=
keyIdea.text: Use non‑blocking assignments in sequential blocks so registers capture current inputs simultaneously and simulation matches hardware.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Non-blocking assignment
Non‑blocking assignment semantics
Right‑hand sides evaluated now; left‑hand sides updated together at the end of the time step.
Concrete contrast
Using blocking assignment in sequential code causes updates to occur immediately and can create unintended sequential dependencies that do not match hardware.
Example scenario
Two registers assigned in the same clocked block will both capture the old values if you use non‑blocking assignment; with blocking assignment the second assignment may see the updated first value leading to incorrect state transitions.
Check your code
  • Search for equals inside always @(posedge clk) and replace with <= unless building combinational temporaries.
  • Keep non‑blocking style consistent across registers to avoid hidden race conditions.
Visual test
Set a=1, b=0, then in a clocked block assign a <= b and b <= a. With non‑blocking they swap simultaneously; with blocking they will not behave like hardware.
Misconception
Some developers think blocking is faster or simpler in clocks — it is not safe for modeling registers.
Key Takeaway

Prefer non‑blocking assignments for all reg updates in clocked always blocks so simulation matches simultaneous hardware updates.

screens.title: Registers and clock enable
screens.narratorSegment: A register in Verilog is a vector of flip‑flops and is usually written as a reg vector that updates in a clocked always block. The common pattern adds an enable signal so the register only updates when a control input is asserted. For instance, an eight‑bit register uses a conditional inside always @(posedge clk) such that if enable is high, q <= d; otherwise q retains its previous value. Synthesis tools typically map that enable to the flip‑flop's native clock enable input on the FPGA, which is efficient for area and timing. The practical example is buffering incoming data until a valid signal asserts enable, avoiding unnecessary switching on other cycles. A misconception is to implement enables by gating the clock externally; clock gating at the RTL level leads to complex timing and is not recommended in FPGA coding styles. Instead, keep the clock clean and use enables inside the flip‑flop logic. For verification, toggle enable and step the clock; with enable low, the register holds its previous value, and with enable high it captures the input. Consider how enables interact with resets: decide whether a reset should clear the register regardless of enable or only when enabled — place the reset check as the highest priority inside the clocked block to implement synchronous resets correctly.

keyIdea.title: Register pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a clocked block with an if (en) q <= d; pattern so hardware clock enables are used rather than gating the clock.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Registers & enables
Enabled register pattern
If enable is asserted, the register captures input on the rising clock; otherwise it holds its value.
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (en)
    q <= d;
end
Synthesis maps en to clock enable on the FPGA's flip‑flops rather than gating the clock signal.
Analogy
Think of enable as a gate that allows the register to listen to its input on the clock edge instead of turning the clock on and off.
Verification scenario
Run a test where en toggles: when en is low the output remains constant across clock edges; when en goes high the output follows the data vector on the next rising edge.
Common mistake
Gating the clock net at RTL to implement enable logic. Keep the clock net intact and express enabling in flip‑flop logic.
Key Takeaway

Use en inside the clocked block so the FPGA’s flip‑flop clock enable is used; never gate the clock at RTL for this purpose.

screens.title: Counters and synchronous reset
screens.narratorSegment: A counter is a register that changes value every clock cycle according to an arithmetic update, often incrementing or decrementing. The typical Verilog pattern places a reset check inside the clocked always block so the reset is synchronous: if reset then count <= 0 else if enable then count <= count + 1. A synchronous reset means the reset takes effect only on a clock edge, which simplifies timing analysis and integrates better with scan and clock gating strategies. For example, an 8‑bit counter with an active‑high synchronous reset will become zero on the next rising edge after rst is asserted. An alternate style is an asynchronous reset, where the always sensitivity list includes the reset, and the flip‑flop is reset immediately when the reset signal asserts. Asynchronous resets can be necessary in some designs, but they complicate timing closure and reset release sequencing. A good verification exercise is to assert reset asynchronously and step clocks to observe differences: synchronous reset waits for the clock edge, asynchronous reset forces an immediate output. Also consider whether the reset should override enable — typically reset is highest priority so it clears the register even if enable is asserted. Understanding these priorities prevents subtle startup bugs in FPGA systems.

keyIdea.title: Reset style
keyIdea.text: Synchronous resets are checked inside the clocked always block and take effect on the clock edge; asynchronous resets act immediately and require careful timing consideration.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Counters & resets
Synchronous counter pattern
Place reset and enable checks inside always @(posedge clk) to implement counters that update predictably with the clock.
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst)
    count <= 8'b0;
  else if (en)
    count <= count + 1'b1;
end
Here reset is synchronous and will clear the counter on the next rising clock after rst asserts.
Comparison
Asynchronous resets act immediately but complicate reset sequencing; synchronous resets are generally preferred in FPGA design for timing and testability.
Verification tip
Test both asserting rst while the clock runs and asserting rst between clock edges. A synchronous reset will only clear at a clock edge; an asynchronous reset clears immediately.
Common pitfall
Assuming reset release timing is trivial. Make sure reset release avoids metastability by following FPGA vendor guidelines.
Key Takeaway

Prefer synchronous resets for predictable timing in FPGAs, and make reset priority explicit inside the clocked block.

screens.title: FSM design patterns: three‑block and two‑block styles
screens.narratorSegment: Finite state machines are expressed in Verilog using a state register and combinational logic for next state and outputs. The recommended three‑block pattern separates concerns: one always @(posedge clk) block for the state register that updates state <= next_state; one always @(*) block for next‑state logic that computes next_state from state and inputs; and one always @(*) block for output logic that derives outputs from the current state. This separation improves readability and reduces accidental latches. A two‑block style collapses next‑state and output logic into a single combinational block and is common for compact designs; it still uses a sequential block for the state register. The traffic light FSM example uses localparam constants to encode states and a two‑block implementation which is concise and clear. When designing your FSM, encode states with localparam so values remain module-local and cannot be overridden. A practical misconception is to mix sequential and combinational assignments in ways that accidentally create latches; always ensure combinational blocks assign every signal on all paths or provide default assignments. For verification, exercise the FSM with input changes and watch outputs — in a Moore machine outputs change only on state transitions at the clock edge, while in a Mealy machine outputs can change immediately with inputs. Consider readability, testability, and timing when choosing between three‑block and two‑block patterns.

keyIdea.title: FSM structure
keyIdea.text: Separate state update, next‑state logic, and outputs for clarity; two‑block style is acceptable for many designs but keep combinational assignments complete.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › FSM design patterns
Three‑block FSM pattern
Clearly separate state register, combinational next‑state, and combinational output logic for robust designs.
Example roles
  • State register: always @(posedge clk) state <= next_state;
  • Next‑state: always @(*) compute next_state from state and inputs.
  • Output logic: always @(*) compute outputs from state (Moore) or from state and inputs (Mealy).
Practical tip
Use localparam for state encodings so they are fixed and non‑overridable, keeping code portable and clear.
Avoiding latches
In combinational blocks give default assignments for signals so every path assigns a value and no implicit latches are inferred by synthesis.
Compact two‑block style
Combine next‑state and outputs into a single combinational block for concise code. Keep the state register sequential. This approach is used in the example traffic light FSM.
Misconception
Thinking two‑block style is inferior — it's fine if combinational logic remains clear and complete with defaults.
Key Takeaway

Choose a clear FSM structure and encode states with localparam; ensure combinational blocks have defaults to avoid latches.

screens.title: Moore vs Mealy machines
screens.narratorSegment: The Moore and Mealy models describe where outputs are generated in an FSM. In a Moore machine outputs depend only on the current state, so they change only when the state changes, which itself happens on a clock edge. This makes Moore outputs synchronous and predictable, which is why Moore machines are often preferred in FPGA design. In contrast, a Mealy machine allows outputs to depend on both state and inputs, so outputs can change immediately when inputs change without waiting for a clock edge. The advantage of Mealy is that it can reduce the number of states needed, and sometimes produce faster response to inputs. The downside is that Mealy outputs can change asynchronously with respect to system clocks and may need extra synchronization when interfacing with other modules. A concrete example is the traffic light FSM: implemented as a Moore machine, the light encoding depends only on the state and updates at the clock edge. A common misconception is that Mealy is always better because it uses fewer states; instead, think about output timing and whether asynchronous changes are acceptable in your system. For practice, convert a small Moore FSM to Mealy and observe how outputs move from clocked changes to input-driven changes, and then consider the synchronization needed when the output crosses clock domains.

keyIdea.title: Moore vs Mealy
keyIdea.text: Moore outputs depend only on state and change on clock edges; Mealy outputs depend on state and inputs and can change immediately with inputs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Moore vs Mealy
Moore machine
Outputs are functions of state only and therefore change on the clock edge when state changes.
Advantage
Predictable synchronous outputs that are easier to interface and time with other modules.
Example
Traffic light outputs assigned from state values so lights update only when state changes on the clock.
Mealy machine
Outputs are functions of state and inputs and can change immediately when inputs change.
Tradeoff
Fewer states possible but outputs may be asynchronous relative to the clock and require synchronization at interfaces.
Practice suggestion

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Traffic light FSM
Code panel
// State encoding
localparam GREEN  = 2'b00;
localparam YELLOW = 2'b01;
localparam RED    = 2'b10;

reg [1:0] state, next_state;

// State register
always @(posedge clk) begin
  if (rst)
    state <= GREEN;
  else
    state <= next_state;
end

// Next-state logic
always @(*) begin
  case (state)
    GREEN:  next_state = timer_done ? YELLOW : GREEN;
    YELLOW: next_state = timer_done ? RED    : YELLOW;
    RED:    next_state = timer_done ? GREEN  : RED;
    default: next_state = GREEN;
  endcase
end

// Output logic (Moore)
always @(*) begin
  case (state)
    GREEN:  light = 3'b100;
    YELLOW: light = 3'b010;
    RED:    light = 3'b001;
    default: light = 3'b100;
  endcase
end
Explanation
  • localparam keeps state constants module-local and immutable.
  • Sequential block uses synchronous reset to set a known start state.
  • Combinational next‑state block calculates next state from current state and timer_done.
  • Output block implements Moore behavior so lights update on state transitions.
Check your understanding
If you add an input that forces immediate yellow as a Mealy output, how would that affect output timing and the need for synchronization?
Key Takeaway

Use localparam encodings, a clear state register, and complete combinational logic to build maintainable FSMs that simulate reliably and map to hardware.

screens.title: Sequence detector: design and simulation task
screens.narratorSegment: The hands‑on activity asks you to design a four‑state sequence detector for the pattern one‑zero‑one‑one on a serial input. The detector should assert detected for one clock cycle when the sequence completes. The recommended approach uses the two‑always‑block style: a sequential block for the state register and a combinational block for next‑state and output logic. Start by drawing the state diagram that represents the longest useful suffixes of the pattern — each state represents how much of the pattern has been matched so far. Encode the states with localparam values and declare a reg for the state and next_state. In the sequential block implement synchronous reset to a known starting state. In the combinational block, use a case statement to define transitions and set detected when the pattern completes. A common mistake is forgetting overlapping matches; ensure the transitions allow the FSM to recognize overlapping occurrences of the pattern. For verification, write a testbench that feeds the sequence 0,1,0,1,1,0,1,1,0 and step the clock for each bit. Check that detected pulses exactly when the four‑bit pattern appears. This exercise links state encoding, sequential update, and combinational transition rules into a single practical example you can simulate quickly to validate your understanding.

screens.title: Why use non‑blocking in sequential blocks? — assessment
screens.narratorSegment: A succinct assessment reinforces the critical distinction between blocking and non‑blocking assignments in sequential always blocks. Ask students first: why should non‑blocking assignments be used in sequential always blocks? The correct answer is that non‑blocking models simultaneous updates of flip‑flops, ensuring that all right‑hand sides are evaluated using current values while left‑hand sides update together at the time step boundary. This matches physical hardware. Follow with a practical exercise: give a short sequential block that mixes blocking and non‑blocking assignments and ask the student to predict simulation behavior versus intended hardware. Another good question contrasts synchronous and asynchronous reset: when does each take effect and what are the timing implications? Students should explain that synchronous reset is applied only on the clock edge and is easier for timing closure in FPGAs, while asynchronous reset acts immediately but needs careful release and synchronizing. Finally, include a code rewrite task: provide a naive implementation that gates the clock for enabling and ask learners to refactor it to use an enable inside the clocked block. These assessments require both conceptual reasoning and hands‑on refactoring, ensuring a deep understanding of sequential Verilog idioms.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the essential concepts you must remember. First, always @(posedge clk) is the canonical way to describe synchronous registers and flip‑flops; model simultaneous updates with non‑blocking assignment so simulation matches hardware. Second, implement registers with an enable inside the clocked block rather than gating the clock; synthesis maps enables efficiently to flip‑flop clock enables. Third, use synchronous resets inside the clocked block for predictable timing unless you have a compelling reason to use asynchronous reset, and place reset as the highest priority inside the sequential block. Fourth, design FSMs using a clear structure: a state register plus combinational next‑state and output logic. Use localparam for state encodings and provide defaults in combinational logic to avoid latches. Finally, choose Moore machines when you want stable, clocked outputs and Mealy machines when you need fewer states or faster input responses, but account for output timing across domains. These ideas form the backbone of reliable FPGA sequential design; carry them into simulations, synthesis, and lab validation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we learn how synchronous behavior is described in Verilog using the always at positive edge of the clock construct. You will see how every assignment to a reg inside a clocked always block implies one or more flip-flops and how non‑blocking assignment models the simultaneous update of hardware. We will walk through concrete modules: a D flip‑flop, an enabled register, an 8‑bit counter with a synchronous reset, and a traffic light finite state machine written in the common two‑block style. You will also learn the recommended three‑block FSM pattern for clarity and when a Moore or a Mealy style is appropriate. Practical implications are emphasized: why synchronous resets are usually preferred in FPGA flows, why localparam is preferred for state encoding, and how to interpret behavior in simulation versus real silicon. By the end you will be ready to design registers, counters, and robust FSMs and to implement a sequence detector as a hands‑on exercise. Think about where simultaneous updates and clocked behavior are crucial in your design — that is the central idea we will return to throughout the lesson.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to express synchronous sequential logic correctly in Verilog and verify it. First, you will write always @(posedge clk) blocks that infer flip‑flops and use non‑blocking assignment so multiple registers update simultaneously. Second, you'll implement registers with clock enables and counters with synchronous resets, understanding how enable and reset signals control captured values in hardware. Third, you'll design finite state machines using the recommended patterns: either the three‑always‑block style for explicit separation of state, next‑state, and outputs, or the common two‑block approach for compact designs. Finally, you'll distinguish Moore and Mealy machines and choose the one that best fits timing and output stability needs. Each objective includes a verification milestone: simulate a D flip‑flop update, test an enabled register with toggled enable, reset and step a counter under a synchronous reset, and simulate the traffic light FSM and a sequence detector to confirm correct outputs. This ensures you not only write code, but also validate timing and behavior in a simulator or on hardware.

Let's expand the objectives into testable checks so you know when you have achieved them. For clocked always blocks, success means writing a D flip‑flop module and observing q follow d only on rising clock edges in simulation. For registers and enables, success is toggling the enable signal while stepping the clock and confirming q holds when enable is low and updates when enable is high. For counters and resets, success is asserting the synchronous reset and seeing the counter return to zero only at a clock edge, and verifying the counter increments when enable is high. For FSMs, success is creating a module where state advances according to inputs and the output encoding matches the state table; simulate a traffic light FSM to observe the expected 001, 010, 100 patterns. For Moore vs Mealy, success is demonstrating an output that either changes only on the clock edge or that can change combinationally with inputs. These verification checks ensure design intent matches both simulation and hardware assumptions.

A clocked always block in Verilog is written as always @(posedge clk) and it tells the simulator and synthesis tools to execute the block at each rising edge of the clock. Practically, every assignment to a reg inside such a block infers a hardware flip‑flop that captures the right‑hand side value at that instant. This is the basic mechanism you use to hold state across cycles. For example, a D flip‑flop module assigns q <= d in an always @(posedge clk) block; when the clock rises, q takes the current value of d. The key reason we use this style is that real flip‑flops on an FPGA capture inputs synchronously on the clock edge; modeling that behavior accurately in code ensures simulation maps to hardware. A common misconception is to think the order of statements inside the block controls update timing—because with non‑blocking assignment all left‑hand sides update simultaneously at the end of the time step. Practically, this means you can compute next‑state expressions using current state and inputs within the same block and rely on simultaneous update semantics to preserve correctness. Consider this teaching check: simulate a D flip‑flop while toggling d asynchronously, and observe q only changes when the clock rises. That observation ties the concept to real behavior and prevents subtle race conditions in complex designs.

Non‑blocking assignment, the <= operator, is essential inside clocked always blocks because it models how hardware updates multiple flip‑flops at the same instant. When you use <=, the right‑hand sides are evaluated immediately using current signals, but the left‑hand sides are updated later, effectively at the end of the simulation time step. This leads to simultaneous capture semantics: two registers assigned in the same block do not see each other's new values in that cycle. For example, if you compute next_a <= b and next_b <= a in the same clocked block, each right‑hand side reads the old values of a and b, and both update together on the clock. A common pitfall is using blocking assignment, equals, inside a sequential block; that causes sequential updates where the second assignment can observe the first's new value and simulation no longer matches hardware. The practical consequence is subtle functional differences and potential combinational loops or unintended data dependencies in simulation. A quick test to reveal this is to implement two registers where one is assigned from the other and toggle the source for a few cycles; using <= will keep behavior consistent and predictable. To summarize, prefer <= in always @(posedge clk) blocks for all reg updates, unless you are explicitly creating temporary combinational variables for next‑state calculation outside of sequential assignments.

A register in Verilog is a vector of flip‑flops and is usually written as a reg vector that updates in a clocked always block. The common pattern adds an enable signal so the register only updates when a control input is asserted. For instance, an eight‑bit register uses a conditional inside always @(posedge clk) such that if enable is high, q <= d; otherwise q retains its previous value. Synthesis tools typically map that enable to the flip‑flop's native clock enable input on the FPGA, which is efficient for area and timing. The practical example is buffering incoming data until a valid signal asserts enable, avoiding unnecessary switching on other cycles. A misconception is to implement enables by gating the clock externally; clock gating at the RTL level leads to complex timing and is not recommended in FPGA coding styles. Instead, keep the clock clean and use enables inside the flip‑flop logic. For verification, toggle enable and step the clock; with enable low, the register holds its previous value, and with enable high it captures the input. Consider how enables interact with resets: decide whether a reset should clear the register regardless of enable or only when enabled — place the reset check as the highest priority inside the clocked block to implement synchronous resets correctly.

A counter is a register that changes value every clock cycle according to an arithmetic update, often incrementing or decrementing. The typical Verilog pattern places a reset check inside the clocked always block so the reset is synchronous: if reset then count <= 0 else if enable then count <= count + 1. A synchronous reset means the reset takes effect only on a clock edge, which simplifies timing analysis and integrates better with scan and clock gating strategies. For example, an 8‑bit counter with an active‑high synchronous reset will become zero on the next rising edge after rst is asserted. An alternate style is an asynchronous reset, where the always sensitivity list includes the reset, and the flip‑flop is reset immediately when the reset signal asserts. Asynchronous resets can be necessary in some designs, but they complicate timing closure and reset release sequencing. A good verification exercise is to assert reset asynchronously and step clocks to observe differences: synchronous reset waits for the clock edge, asynchronous reset forces an immediate output. Also consider whether the reset should override enable — typically reset is highest priority so it clears the register even if enable is asserted. Understanding these priorities prevents subtle startup bugs in FPGA systems.

Finite state machines are expressed in Verilog using a state register and combinational logic for next state and outputs. The recommended three‑block pattern separates concerns: one always @(posedge clk) block for the state register that updates state <= next_state; one always @(*) block for next‑state logic that computes next_state from state and inputs; and one always @(*) block for output logic that derives outputs from the current state. This separation improves readability and reduces accidental latches. A two‑block style collapses next‑state and output logic into a single combinational block and is common for compact designs; it still uses a sequential block for the state register. The traffic light FSM example uses localparam constants to encode states and a two‑block implementation which is concise and clear. When designing your FSM, encode states with localparam so values remain module-local and cannot be overridden. A practical misconception is to mix sequential and combinational assignments in ways that accidentally create latches; always ensure combinational blocks assign every signal on all paths or provide default assignments. For verification, exercise the FSM with input changes and watch outputs — in a Moore machine outputs change only on state transitions at the clock edge, while in a Mealy machine outputs can change immediately with inputs. Consider readability, testability, and timing when choosing between three‑block and two‑block patterns.

The Moore and Mealy models describe where outputs are generated in an FSM. In a Moore machine outputs depend only on the current state, so they change only when the state changes, which itself happens on a clock edge. This makes Moore outputs synchronous and predictable, which is why Moore machines are often preferred in FPGA design. In contrast, a Mealy machine allows outputs to depend on both state and inputs, so outputs can change immediately when inputs change without waiting for a clock edge. The advantage of Mealy is that it can reduce the number of states needed, and sometimes produce faster response to inputs. The downside is that Mealy outputs can change asynchronously with respect to system clocks and may need extra synchronization when interfacing with other modules. A concrete example is the traffic light FSM: implemented as a Moore machine, the light encoding depends only on the state and updates at the clock edge. For practice, convert a small Moore FSM to Mealy and observe how outputs move from clocked changes to input-driven changes, and then consider the synchronization needed when the output crosses clock domains.
